parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: English Opening: King's English Variation
parent.overview: After 1.c4 e5 White has what is in effect a Sicilian Defence with colours reversed and an extra tempo (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads with very different set-ups: the Botvinnik System (c4, Nc3, g3, Bg2, d3, e4, Nge2) is a slow bind on d5; the Four Knights (2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6) and 3.g3 lines give fianchetto systems; the Flohr-Mikenas-type 3.e4 and 2.Nc3 Nf6 with an early d4 are sharper (s1, s2, s4). White's recurring themes are control of d5, queenside expansion with b4 and Rb1, and the long diagonal (s2, s4). Black neutralises the extra tempo with ...d5 breaks, ...f5 or an early ...Bb4 (s2). Overall the play is flexible and manoeuvring with little forcing theory (s1, s2), though the Four Knights in this move order is described as sharper than its 1.e4 cousin (s4).

root.name: Ruy Lopez: Retreat Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Nb8

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.
